newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ dlr grossly overvalued - Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ dlr grossly overvalued - Goldman Sachs.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar is grossly overvalued and could potentially be in for a quick and nasty correction, said Jim O'Neill, chief currency economist with U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs, on Friday.
Goldman has for 18 months held that the "kiwi" was overvalued, but it has sustained its merry upward path.
"The longer a currency stays grossly misaligned, ultimately, the quicker and nastier the correction will be," said O'Neill, visiting New Zealand to talk to officials and private sector analysts.
Goldman argues the kiwi is 15 percent overvalued against the U.S. dollar and the Trade-Weighted Index, over 20 percent against the mark and nearly 25 percent against the yen.
"We are forecasting in 12 months that the kiwi is going to be down at 65 U.S. cents," O'Neill told Reuters.
The kiwi was at 69.3 U.S. cents on Friday.
O'Neill stresses Goldman is not advising investors to aggressively sell New Zealand dollar assets -- just to hedge.

"For long-term investors, we would not recommend them having unhedged positions in New Zealand because the upside potential for the New Zealand dollar seems purely based on the nominal interest rate differential remaining."

O'Neill expects the differential for New Zealand's nominal rates to close against the U.S. as the Federal Reserve tightens again this year and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RB) holds or eases monetary conditions.
Next Tuesday's March quarter inflation data will be a key.
"If next week's inflation data comes through below the Reserve Bank's forecast of 0.5 percent, the case for the exchange rate to start weakening, encouraged by the central bank, is going to grow.
"That's what I have picked up while I have been here -- I think that is highly likely."
So why is Goldman so bearish on the kiwi?

The growing current account deficit -- forecast by the RB to rise from 4.6 percent of GDP to 5.9 percent in 1999 -- is one reason. The deficit has resulted from a sharp fall in New Zealand's trade balance from a surplus of two percent of GDP to
a forecast small deficit.
The current account deficit this year is probably going to be the highest in the OECD, said O'Neill.
Finance Minister Bill Birch said this week that export volume growth in 1996 suggested the currency was not overvalued, but O'Neill has seen anecdotal evidence to support the Goldman view.
"Every time I look at any primary industry, whether it be wool or dairy or pig farming, the anecdotal complaints from those industries are very strong."
He said exports were strong because of strength in the U.S. economy but should be much stronger.

He said Prime Minister Jim Bolger was right in the long run in arguing a strong currency implied a strong economy, but that did not presently apply to New Zealand, where productivity growth had been "incredibly weak".
"The kiwi strength has gone way and beyond anything justified by inflation or productivity differentials."
For O'Neill, investment intentions were the key data to watch. If Goldman's model was right, investment intentions should fall sharply in coming months.
A current account build-up mainly associated with growing public and private sector consumption would be disturbing.
"If investment turns out to be a lot stronger in the next 12 months then it would appear to suggest that our model is wrong."
O'Neill said that the RB, having used the exchange rate to quell the economy last year, had started to focus on the current account as a way of managing the currency down.
He even suggested the bank might at present be advised to discourage foreign bond investors, to smooth the kiwi's demise.
High interest rates had attracted hot money and "at some stage it comes to a rather ugly halt if it is not supported by the underlying balance of payments position.
"(RB Governor Don) Brash and his colleagues should be a little bit bolder in trying to bring down the kiwi strength."
O'Neill said the RB could afford a lower currency if its forecast of sharply falling inflation is correct.
Historically, high interest rates were generally used to support weak currencies and eventually New Zealand's rates would have to come down, O'Neill said.
"If New Zealand is ultimately to stay as prosperous as the last decade has allowed it to develop, it really needs low interest rates and a competitive exchange rate.
"Countries can't live with misaligned exchange rates for too long."
